questions.stem: A previously healthy young adult client develops sudden, sharp unilateral chest pain and shortness of breath with no preceding trauma, and a family member immediately assumes this must be a heart attack given the chest pain. The nurse should instead suspect:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A chest wall strain causing reproducible pain without acute respiratory compromise","B":"A urinary infection causing dysuria rather than abrupt unilateral chest symptoms","C":"A spontaneous pneumothorax causing sudden unilateral pleuritic pain and dyspnea","D":"A myocardial infarction diagnosed solely from age and the presence of chest pain"}}
questions.rationale: Sudden, sharp unilateral chest pain and dyspnea with no preceding trauma, particularly in a young, otherwise healthy adult (classically tall and thin), raises suspicion for spontaneous pneumothorax, warranting further evaluation, such as chest X-ray, to confirm and guide treatment.

questions.stem: A young child presents with high fever, drooling, absence of a cough, and a preference for sitting upright leaning forward (tripod position). The nurse should recognize this as a possible sign of:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An allergic rash without evidence of upper-airway compromise or respiratory distress","B":"An uncomplicated viral cold that requires only routine home supportive treatment","C":"Viral croup causing a barking cough and stridor without the classic drooling pattern","D":"Epiglottitis causing drooling and tripod positioning with a threatened upper airway"}}
questions.rationale: Drooling without a barking cough, high fever, and the tripod position are classic, highly concerning signs of epiglottitis, a life-threatening airway emergency. The nurse must avoid attempting to examine the throat, use a tongue depressor, or upset the child, since this can precipitate complete airway obstruction; emergency airway management should be arranged immediately.
questions.source_name: NCBI Bookshelf — Epiglottitis
questions.source_detail: Pediatric presentation and emergency management: drooling/tripod position; avoid throat instrumentation before airway control; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A young child presents with a high fever lasting more than 5 days, along with red eyes (without discharge), a rash, swollen red hands/feet, and a "strawberry tongue." The nurse should suspect:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A benign childhood exanthem that needs no additional clinical assessment or follow-up","B":"An uncomplicated viral syndrome requiring only routine symptomatic home treatment","C":"A medication allergy that fully explains prolonged fever plus mucocutaneous findings","D":"Kawasaki disease requiring prompt evaluation because coronary complications can occur"}}
questions.rationale: Prolonged fever (5+ days) combined with conjunctival injection (without discharge), rash, extremity changes (swelling, redness), and strawberry tongue are classic features of Kawasaki disease, a systemic vasculitis of childhood requiring prompt recognition and treatment (typically IVIG), given the significant risk of coronary artery aneurysms if left untreated.

questions.stem: A client with anaphylaxis receives an initial dose of intramuscular epinephrine, but symptoms do not adequately improve after several minutes, and a new team member assumes no more epinephrine can be given no matter what. The nurse should instead anticipate:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Repeat intramuscular epinephrine per protocol when anaphylaxis persists or recurs","B":"Avoid all additional epinephrine after the first intramuscular dose is administered","C":"Wait at least one hour before giving any further treatment for persistent symptoms","D":"Use an oral antihistamine alone instead of repeating epinephrine for ongoing symptoms"}}
questions.rationale: If symptoms of anaphylaxis do not adequately improve after an initial dose of epinephrine, current guidelines support administering a repeat dose (commonly after about 5-15 minutes, per protocol) since a single dose may be insufficient, particularly in severe reactions, and this should not be delayed by relying on antihistamines or other adjunct treatments alone.

questions.source_detail: Management section: repeat intramuscular epinephrine for persistent symptoms at guideline intervals; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A client's echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 30%, and a family member assumes this number sounds fairly normal since it's not zero. The nurse should recognize this value as:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An ejection fraction of 30% is markedly reduced and falls within the HFrEF range","B":"An ejection fraction of 30% is unrelated to left ventricular systolic performance","C":"An ejection fraction of 30% is within the normal expected range for most adults","D":"An ejection fraction of 30% is above the normal range and indicates hyperdynamic flow"}}
questions.rationale: Normal ejection fraction is generally considered to be approximately 50-70%. A value of 30% is significantly reduced, consistent with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), reflecting impaired systolic pumping function of the heart.

questions.stem: A nurse is monitoring central venous pressure (CVP) in a critically ill client. Which interpretation of CVP is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"CVP primarily estimates right atrial pressure and must be interpreted with other data","B":"CVP directly measures kidney filtration and independently determines renal function","C":"CVP reliably measures total circulating volume and accurately predicts fluid response","D":"CVP directly measures left ventricular filling pressure and pulmonary venous pressure"}}
questions.rationale: CVP approximates pressure near the right atrium and can contribute to assessment of right-sided hemodynamics. It is influenced by volume status, venous compliance, intrathoracic pressure, and cardiac function, so CVP alone should not be treated as a reliable measure of total blood volume or fluid responsiveness.

questions.source_detail: Introduction/Issues of Concern: CVP estimates right atrial pressure/preload but is a poor standalone predictor of fluid responsiveness; updated 2023-07-10, StatPearls 2026 edition; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.rationale: Pulmonary artery wedge pressure (PAWP), obtained via a pulmonary artery (Swan-Ganz) catheter, is used to estimate left atrial pressure and left ventricular filling pressure (preload), providing valuable information about left heart function and fluid status in critically ill clients, particularly useful in differentiating cardiogenic from non-cardiogenic causes of pulmonary edema.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews an arterial blood gas result showing a significantly negative base excess (base deficit). The nurse should recognize this finding as suggestive of:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A negative base excess reflects a metabolic acidifying component or relative base deficit","B":"A negative base excess indicates an isolated respiratory disorder with no metabolic role","C":"A negative base excess represents normal acid-base balance despite a markedly low value","D":"A negative base excess is clinically unrelated to metabolic acid-base interpretation"}}
questions.rationale: Base excess (or base deficit, when negative) reflects the metabolic component of acid-base balance. A significantly negative base excess (base deficit) suggests a metabolic acidosis component, indicating a relative deficit of buffering base, often seen in conditions such as lactic acidosis, DKA, or renal failure.

questions.stem: A nurse is monitoring a critically ill client's mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2). A significantly low SvO2 value generally indicates:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Low SvO2 can reflect increased tissue extraction when oxygen delivery is inadequate","B":"Low SvO2 indicates oxygen delivery is excessive relative to current metabolic demand","C":"Low SvO2 is a normal finding that does not require hemodynamic clinical correlation","D":"Low SvO2 is unrelated to the balance between oxygen delivery and tissue consumption"}}
questions.rationale: A low mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) indicates that tissues are extracting more oxygen than usual from the blood, often reflecting inadequate oxygen delivery relative to tissue demand — which can occur in states of low cardiac output, significant anemia, or increased metabolic demand — prompting further hemodynamic assessment and intervention.

questions.stem: A mechanically ventilated client receives regular oral care that includes toothbrushing. Why is toothbrushing clinically relevant even though the client is not eating by mouth?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Regular toothbrushing helps reduce dental plaque and oral bacterial burden in hospital care","B":"Regular toothbrushing replaces the need for suctioning in mechanically ventilated patients","C":"Regular toothbrushing is performed mainly for appearance without a meaningful health role","D":"Regular toothbrushing should be avoided because it increases pneumonia risk in the hospital"}}
questions.rationale: Dental plaque can contain pathogenic bacteria, and plaque rapidly reforms without mechanical oral hygiene. Regular toothbrushing helps reduce plaque and oral bacterial burden. Oral care is part of pneumonia-prevention practice, but it does not replace suctioning or other ventilator-care measures.

questions.stem: A nurse is differentiating between malingering and factitious disorder for a client whose symptoms seem to have appeared right around the time a disability claim was filed. The key distinguishing feature of malingering, relevant to this particular timing, is:

questions.rationale: Malingering involves the intentional production of symptoms motivated by an identifiable external incentive (such as financial compensation, avoiding work/legal responsibility, or obtaining medications), distinguishing it from factitious disorder, in which the motivation is understood to be primarily psychological rather than tied to external gain. Malingering itself is not classified as a mental disorder in the DSM-5-TR, but rather as a condition that may be a focus of clinical attention.

questions.stem: A nurse is explaining the difference between an H2 receptor blocker (such as famotidine) and a proton pump inhibitor (such as omeprazole) to a client who assumes the two medications basically work the exact same way. The nurse should instead explain that:

questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Keep the auto-injector indefinitely because epinephrine does not lose potency with time","B":"Store the auto-injector in extreme heat or cold because temperature does not affect it","C":"Check expiration and solution appearance regularly and replace the device when indicated","D":"Use the auto-injector even when the solution is cloudy, discolored, or contains particles"}}
questions.rationale: Clients should be taught to regularly check the expiration date of their epinephrine auto-injector and replace it before expiration, since expired epinephrine may have reduced potency and effectiveness during a life-threatening anaphylactic reaction. The device should also be stored at controlled room temperature and inspected for discoloration or particulates, which would indicate it should be replaced.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Epinephrine Auto-Injector
questions.source_detail: Storage/handling: controlled room temperature, inspect solution, replace if discolored/cloudy/particulate and replace before expiration; revised 2023-02; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A client is prescribed a transdermal clonidine patch for hypertension, and mentions a plan to apply it to a small area of skin that's currently a bit irritated from a recent scrape, thinking it wouldn't make much difference. The nurse should teach the client to instead:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Apply the clonidine patch directly over broken or irritated skin to increase absorption","B":"Replace the clonidine patch every day because the transdermal dose lasts only 24 hours","C":"Apply to clean, dry, intact hairless skin and replace on the labeled weekly schedule","D":"Cut the clonidine patch into smaller pieces whenever a lower dose is desired"}}
questions.rationale: Transdermal clonidine patches should be applied to a clean, dry, hairless area of intact skin, changed per the product's specific labeled interval (often weekly), with site rotation to reduce skin irritation. Patches should not be cut, and application to broken or irritated skin should be avoided, since this can alter drug absorption.

questions.source_detail: Current FDA label listing for Catapres-TTS transdermal system; apply to intact hairless skin and replace on the labeled 7-day schedule; FDA label current 2026; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A nurse is responsible for maintaining proper vaccine storage in a clinic refrigerator, and a new hire assumes the temperature really only matters during shipping from the manufacturer, not once it's sitting in the clinic. questions.rationale: Vaccines are sensitive biological products that require maintenance of an unbroken "cold chain" (appropriate temperature range) from manufacture through administration, since exposure to temperatures outside the recommended range (too warm or, for some vaccines, freezing) can reduce potency and effectiveness, potentially compromising the vaccine's ability to provide adequate immunity.
questions.source_name: CDC — Storage and Handling of Immunobiologics

questions.rationale: Needle gauge selection should consider the viscosity of the medication (thicker solutions may require a larger-diameter, lower-gauge-number needle to allow adequate flow), the injection route/site, and client-specific factors such as body size, to ensure both effective medication delivery and client comfort/safety.

questions.rationale: CDC states that adult peripheral IV catheters do not need routine replacement more frequently than every 72–96 hours and lists clinically indicated-only replacement in adults as an unresolved issue. questions.stem: A new nurse states that hand hygiene is unnecessary as long as gloves are worn. The charge nurse should correct this misconception by explaining:

questions.rationale: Wearing gloves does not eliminate the need for hand hygiene. questions.stem: A provider orders a trough drug level to be drawn at a specific time relative to the client's next medication dose, and a new nurse draws the sample an hour early since the unit happened to be quiet at that moment. questions.stem: A post-operative client reports a sudden "popping" sensation at the surgical incision, followed by increased drainage and visible separation of the wound edges, with abdominal organs protruding. The nurse's priority actions include:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Cover exposed organs with sterile saline-moistened dressings and notify the surgeon urgently","B":"Cover exposed tissue with a dry nonsterile dressing and reassess at the end of the shift","C":"Attempt to push protruding organs back into the abdomen before notifying the surgical team","D":"Ambulate the client immediately so movement can reduce tension around the open incision"}}
questions.rationale: Wound evisceration is a surgical emergency. Priority actions include covering the wound and protruding organs with a sterile saline-soaked dressing (never attempting to push organs back in), positioning the client to reduce abdominal tension (often low Fowler's with knees bent), keeping the client NPO in anticipation of emergency surgery, and notifying the surgeon immediately.

questions.stem: A post-operative client reports abdominal distention, nausea, and absence of bowel sounds and flatus several days after abdominal surgery, and a family member assumes this must mean the surgical wound itself has become infected. The nurse should instead suspect:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A surgical wound infection causing absent bowel sounds as its defining postoperative sign","B":"Normal postoperative recovery that requires no assessment despite persistent distention","C":"A urinary tract infection causing absent bowel sounds, nausea, and lack of flatus","D":"Postoperative ileus causing impaired bowel motility with distention and absent flatus"}}
questions.rationale: Abdominal distention, nausea, and absence of bowel sounds/flatus following abdominal surgery are classic signs of postoperative ileus, a temporary impairment of normal bowel motility. While mild ileus is common after abdominal surgery, persistent or worsening symptoms warrant further assessment, since prolonged ileus can lead to complications and may occasionally indicate a more serious issue such as mechanical obstruction.

questions.stem: A postoperative client has new mild dyspnea with reduced breath sounds at the lung bases after shallow breathing and limited mobility. The nurse should suspect:

questions.rationale: Postoperative atelectasis can produce dyspnea and decreased breath sounds, especially with shallow ventilation and immobility. Lung-expansion measures and mobilization may be used as clinically appropriate. Fever should not be used as a defining cue because evidence does not support atelectasis as a cause of postoperative fever.
